title: Osteosarcopenia Predicts Mortality in Metastatic Prostate Cancer: A Longitudinal Analysis of Opportunistic CT Imaging
abstract: Background: /Objectives: Osteoporosis and sarcopenia are associated with fractures, falls, and mortality. In prostate cancer, aging, advanced disease, and androgen deprivation therapy may accelerate concurrent bone and muscle loss. This study characterized longitudinal CT-derived musculoskeletal biomarkers in metastatic prostate cancer and evaluated the association between baseline osteosarcopenia and overall survival. Methods: This retrospective single-centre cohort included patients treated from 2009 to 2022, with follow-up imaging through 2024. An automated deep-learning pipeline quantified lumbar trabecular bone mineral density (BMD), psoas muscle volume (PV), psoas muscle density (PD), and volumetric psoas muscle index (vPMI). Osteosarcopenia was defined as concurrent osteoporosis (BMD < 135 HU) and sarcopenia (vPMI < 30). Survival from baseline CT was assessed using Kaplan-Meier analysis and multivariable Cox regression. Results: Among 437 patients with 3389 CT scans, osteoporosis, sarcopenia, and osteosarcopenia increased from 29.6%, 46.9%, and 17.2% at baseline to 54.0%, 82.8%, and 45.5% at final imaging. BMD declined by 2.1-3.7% annually, PD by 3.2-3.9%, and PV by 3.6-4.6% (all p < 0.0001). In the final year of life, PD declined by 12.0% and PV by 9.3%. Baseline osteosarcopenia remained independently associated with mortality after adjustment for age, time from diagnosis to baseline CT, PSA, and Gleason risk group (HR 2.11, 95% CI 1.50-2.99; p < 0.001). Conclusions: Osteosarcopenia is common and progressive in metastatic prostate cancer, and muscle loss accelerates near death. Baseline osteosarcopenia independently identifies patients at increased mortality risk. Automated analysis of routine surveillance CT may enable longitudinal musculoskeletal assessment and prognostic risk stratification.

title: Distilling Multimodal Biomedical Foundation Models for Edge Tuberculosis Screening: Client-Side WebAssembly Deployment and Conformal Clinical Abstention
abstract: Background: Deep learning for tuberculosis triage risks shortcut learning and overconfidence. We evaluate distilling BioMedCLIP into an edge-deployable architecture with a selective conformal safety interlock. Methods: A DenseNet-121 student (7.74M parameters) was trained on 12,599 radiographs via Tri-Loss distillation from a frozen BioMedCLIP teacher (86.4M parameters). Validation evaluated 3,441 radiographs: a primary within-scanner clinical benchmark (Combined India: Solan N=155, NITRD N=278) and an adversarial compression stress-test (Pakistan N=3,008). Mondrian split-conformal prediction calibrated a three-tiered interlock: urgent molecular testing, autonomous clearance, and clinical referral. Findings: Distillation significantly outperformed the supervised baseline: Solan AUROC 0.9449 vs 0.8613; NITRD AUROC 0.9520 vs 0.8718; Combined India AUROC 0.9497 vs 0.8635; and Pakistan AUROC 0.8624 vs 0.4990 (all p < 0.0001). In Indian hospital cohorts, the system referred 63.1% of ambiguous active TB cases to clinicians, flagging 32.5% as urgent for GeneXpert testing, while autonomously clearing 77.4% of healthy controls (178/230). Against total screening volume (3,441 external scans), the interlock achieved an unconditional false-clearance rate of 0.26% (9/3,441; 0.00% on cavitary MDR-TB development proxy). Among confirmed active TB cases, the false-negative discharge rate was 4.4% in India (9/203, down from 16.3% on baseline) and 0.0% in Pakistan (0/2,494), counterbalanced by 63.1% clinical referral. Pure graph execution latency of the 27.0 MB WebAssembly model was 77.5 ms on reference x86_64 CPU. Interpretation: Distilling foundation models into selective classification networks reconciles diagnostic accuracy with edge efficiency. Rather than forcing uncalibrated decisions, the system clears normal scans, expedites molecular assays for high-confidence TB, and safely refers diagnostic ambiguity to clinicians. Funding: Independent departmental resources; no external commercial funding.

In Indian hospital cohorts, the system referred 63.1% of ambiguous active TB cases to clinicians, flagging 32.5% as urgent for GeneXpert testing, while autonomously clearing 77.4% of healthy controls (178/230). Against total screening volume (3,441 external scans), the interlock achieved an unconditional false-clearance rate of 0.26% (9/3,441; 0.00% on cavitary MDR-TB development proxy). Among confirmed active TB cases, the false-negative discharge rate was 4.4% in India (9/203, down from 16.3% on baseline) and 0.0% in Pakistan (0/2,494), counterbalanced by 63.1% clinical referral. Pure graph execution latency of the 27.0 MB WebAssembly model was 77.5 ms on reference x86_64 CPU. Interpretation: Distilling foundation models into selective classification networks reconciles diagnostic accuracy with edge efficiency. Rather than forcing uncalibrated decisions, the system clears normal scans, expedites molecular assays for high-confidence TB, and safely refers diagnostic ambiguity to clinicians. title: AI-Driven Retinal Screening: A Stacked Machine Learning Framework for Automated Diabetic Retinopathy Detection in Routine Medical Checkups Using a Public Fundus Database
abstract: Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is a leading cause of preventable blindness, yet large numbers of people with diabetes miss their annual eye examination because grading retinal photographs requires scarce specialists. This paper proposes an artificial intelligence (AI) based eye-inspection framework that embeds automated DR screening inside a routine general medical checkup. The framework comprises five layers: image acquisition, automated quality control, lesion feature extraction, a stacked machine learning (ML) decision engine, and an explainable clinical report with referral. We evaluate the approach on the public UCI Diabetic Retinopathy Debrecen database, which contains 19 lesion, anatomical and image-level features extracted from 1,151 MESSIDOR fundus images. Nine classical and neural classifiers are benchmarked with 10-fold stratified cross-validation, after which the proposed pipeline adds lesion-aware feature engineering, hyperparameter tuning and stacked generalization. The proposed model reaches a cross-validated area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.854 and accuracy of 77.6%, improving the logistic-regression baseline by 0.029 AUC, and achieves a hold-out AUC of 0.878 (95% bootstrap CI 0.830–0.917) with 79.7% sensitivity and 77.6% specificity. Lowering the decision threshold to 0.30 yields 91.9% sensitivity for screening use. In an extension to cataract, three image-clarity features separate normal from cataract fundus images with a cross-validated AUC of 0.978. Permutation importance and ablation show that microaneurysm counts carry most of the diagnostic signal, consistent with clinical grading. Using CDC surveillance data covering 9.6 million Americans with DR, we project that the screening operating point would detect 8.8 million cases while removing about 16 million specialist grading visits per year. We discuss clinical workflow integration, challenges including domain shift, bias and regulation, and a roadmap towards deep-learning-based multi-disease retinal screening.

title: Detector-Stage Failures in Box-Prompted Glioma Segmentation: A Three-Arm Analysis Across Two External Cohorts
abstract: Background: /Objectives: Whether the detector or the segmenter fails externally is unknown in a box-prompted pipeline; an oracle-box arm separates them by prompting with the ground-truth box. Methods: A real-time detection transformer (RT-DETR) with Segment Anything Model (SAM) 2.1 was evaluated against MedSAM3 with a low-rank adaptation (LoRA) adapter on 158 glioma cases from three cohorts. Three arms decompose the gap into a detector-stage term and a residual; a fourth splits the residual. Results: At whole tumour the cost of finding the box rises from +0.006 Dice in domain to +0.091 on the Brain Tumour Segmentation (BraTS) Africa cohort, a difference of +0.085 [+0.045, +0.130] that survives a second detector seed and a second segmenter. The Río Hortega University Hospital glioblastoma cohort (RHUH-GBM) did not show a statistically resolved increase; the two external cohorts differ by +0.073 [+0.035, +0.116]. On BraTS-Africa, slices with no box carry the term, not poorly placed boxes. The in-domain baseline is not categorical: the term excludes zero under a matched prompt and on tumour core. Nine of 95 pipeline cases fall below 0.5 Dice; a post hoc coverage flag identifies seven. Conclusions: On BraTS-Africa, but not RHUH-GBM, the increase in pipeline deficit was primarily associated with the detector stage.

title: Biocompatibility and Osseointegration of Plasma-Anodized Additively Manufactured Co–Cr–Mo Implants in a Rat Critical-Size Calvarial Defect Model
abstract: Background: Additive manufacturing has emerged as a promising technology for the fabrication of patient-specific metallic implants with complex architectures for craniofacial reconstruction. Among metallic biomaterials, cobalt–chromium–molybdenum (Co–28Cr–6Mo) alloys exhibit excellent mechanical strength and corrosion resistance. Plasma anodization has been proposed as a surface engineering strategy to enhance the biological performance of metallic implants; how-ever, its ability to improve osseointegration and bone regeneration remains uncertain. This study investigated the biological response of plasma-anodized additively manufactured Co–28Cr–6Mo implants in a rat critical-size calvarial defect model. Methods: Forty-eight male Wistar rats were randomly assigned to eight experimental groups (n = 6 per group) receiving untreated Co–28Cr–6Mo implants, plasma-anodized Co–28Cr–6Mo implants, titanium-coated plas-ma-anodized Co–28Cr–6Mo implants, or empty defects (control). Animals were euthanized after 6 or 12 weeks. Biological performance was assessed by macroscopic and radiographic examina-tions, histological analyses (Stevens Blue and Von Kossa staining), and quantitative histomor-phometric evaluation of newly formed bone area. Results: All implant surfaces demonstrated excellent in vivo biocompatibility, with no evidence of chronic inflammation, implant rejection, corrosion, or postoperative complications throughout the experimental period. Histological analyses consistently revealed limited bone formation confined to the margins of the defects and the persistence of fibrous connective tissue between the implant surface and the host bone. Quan-titative histomorphometry showed a slight increase in newly formed bone after 12 weeks com-pared with 6 weeks; however, no statistically significant differences were observed among the Control, Co–28Cr–6Mo, Co–28Cr–6Mo PIII, and Co–28Cr–6Mo/Ti PIII groups (p > 0.05). Conclu-sions: Plasma anodization preserved the excellent biocompatibility of additively manufactured Co–28Cr–6Mo implants but did not significantly improve osseointegration or bone regeneration in a rat critical-size calvarial defect model. These findings indicate that plasma anodization alone is insufficient to enhance the regenerative performance of Co–Cr–Mo implants and suggest that additional bioactive surface functionalization strategies may be necessary to promote bone re-pair in critical-size craniofacial defects.

title: Detection and Decision-Making for Secondary Caries: A Scoping Review Informing a Clinical Decision Framework
abstract: Background: Secondary caries or caries around restorations or sealants is a common reason for replacement of restorations. However, distinguishing true secondary caries from restoration-related defects remains clinically difficult and may lead to overtreatment and unnecessary removal of healthy tooth structure. Objectives: This scoping review aimed to map how diagnostic strategies for secondary caries are used and how these findings are translated into treatment decisions, while identifying diagnostic thresholds and informing an evidence-based decision framework. Methods: Searches were performed in seven electronic databases, gray literature sources, and guideline repositories without restrictions on language or publication year. Evidence addressing diagnostic strategies for secondary caries, as well as relevant guidelines and consensus documents, were included. Data were organized descriptively, and the methodological quality of primary studies was critically evaluated. Results: Forty-eight documents were included (34 original studies and 14 guidelines or consensus statements). Visual–tactile examination, commonly combined with bitewings, was the most frequently reported detection approach. Adjunctive methods, including fluorescence-based devices, optical imaging, and artificial intelligence, were investigated as complementary detection tools, with heterogeneous performance across study designs. Treatment decisions were primarily driven by lesion activity and suspected dentine involvement rather than marginal appearance alone. Explicit diagnostic thresholds were rarely predefined, and substantial variability was observed in how diagnostic findings informed treatment decisions. Conclusions: The evidence supports visual–tactile assessment complemented by bitewings as first-line approaches within a diagnostic strategy for secondary caries evaluation. However, heterogeneity in diagnostic thresholds and treatment decision criteria limits comparability across studies and may contribute to inconsistent clinical management. Greater standardization in reporting diagnostic strategies and decision frameworks is needed to support evidence-based and conservative care. Clinical significance: This review provides an evidence-informed clinical framework based on visual–tactile and radiographic assessment for secondary caries around restorations. By integrating detection methods, lesion interpretation, and commonly reported clinical thresholds, the framework illustrates how findings from routine assessment are translated into treatment strategies. The findings indicate that treatment decisions are more consistently guided by lesion activity and dentine involvement than by restoration defects alone, supporting a more conservative approach under diagnostic uncertainty and highlighting the need for greater standardization in clinical criteria.

title: Complementary Predictive Values of the Glasgow Coma Scale–Pupils Score and Rotterdam CT Score for Outcomes in Adults With Acute Epidural Hematoma and Glasgow Coma Scale of 8 or Lower
abstract: Abstract Objective This study aimed to evaluate the prognostic factors associated with 6-month mortality and functional outcomes in adult patients with severe acute epidural hematoma (AEDH; GCS ≤ 8), focusing on comparing the predictive performance of the Glasgow Coma Scale–Pupils (GCS-P) score and the Rotterdam computed tomography (CT) score. Methods We retrospectively analyzed data from 84 adults with severe AEDH (GCS ≤ 8) registered in the Korean Neurotrauma Data Bank System. Multivariable logistic regression and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analyses were performed. For GCS-P score ROC analysis, the analysis direction was set to detect adverse events with lower scores (lower GCS-P values as the positive class) to ensure reproducibility. Paired areas under the receiver operating characteristic curves (AUCs) were compared using DeLong’s test. Results At 6 months, the mortality rate was 22.6% (n = 19), and 40.5% (n = 34) had unfavorable functional outcomes, defined as a Glasgow Outcome Scale-Extended (GOSE) score of 1–4. In multivariable analysis, the Rotterdam score was an independent predictor of 6-month mortality (OR = 1.972, p = 0.0226), while the GCS-P score was a strong independent predictor of both mortality (OR = 0.660, p = 0.0293) and unfavorable functional outcome (OR = 0.519, p = 0.0002). ROC analysis showed acceptable and comparable mortality prediction for both the Rotterdam score (AUC = 0.759, 95% CI: 0.633–0.872) and GCS-P score (AUC = 0.739, 95% CI: 0.606–0.857; DeLong's p = 0.814). However, for predicting unfavorable functional outcome, the GCS-P score (AUC = 0.764, 95% CI: 0.648–0.865) demonstrated statistically significant superiority over the Rotterdam score (AUC = 0.641, 95% CI: 0.522–0.757; DeLong's p = 0.046) Conclusion The GCS-P and Rotterdam CT scores provide distinct and complementary prognostic value. The Rotterdam score is highly effective for acute mortality risk stratification by reflecting morphological mass effect, whereas the GCS-P score offers superior accuracy in predicting long-term functional recovery. Clinical trial number Not applicable.

title: OCT evaluation as a prognostic indicator for management of macular edema secondary to venous occlusion treated with Ranibizumab
abstract: Abstract Aim: To study OCT characteristics as a prognostic guide in macular edema secondary to non-ischemic central retinal vein occlusion treated with intravitreal Ranibizumab Materials and methods: 60 patients with macular edema secondary to non-ischemic central retinal vein occlusion treated with Ranibizumab OCT analyzed on pattern of macular edema, reflectivity of outer band of photoreceptor-RPE complex. Its bearing on visual prognosis was analyzed. RESULTS: Good reflectivity of outer layer is a good prognostic feature. Cystoid pattern is a better prognostic indicator than sub retinal fluid Conclusion: The type of macular edema and reflectivity of third high reflectivity band before treatment can be predictive of visual outcome

title: Enhanced anti-tumor efficacy of Electrochemotherapy combined with marginal surgery in dogs with Mast Cell Tumors and Soft Tissue Sarcomas
abstract: Abstract Background and Objectives Electrochemotherapy (ECT) has emerged as an effective treatment modality for various tumor types in both preclinical and clinical settings within human and veterinary Oncology. We sought to evaluate the effect of electrochemotherapy (ECT) on survival of companion dogs with mast cell tumors and soft tissue sarcomas as an adjuvant to surgery. Materials and Methods A single-institution retrospective case series evaluation was used to identify dogs with mast cell tumors and soft tissue sarcomas undergoing surgical resection followed by electrochemotherapy from 2020–2024. Patients were selected based on having both therapies and categorized by histopathology. ECT was combined post-surgery with IV bleomycin and IL cisplatin in all cases. Overall response rate, survival and recurrence was analyzed. Results A total of 605 patients were identified as having surgery with incomplete margins followed by electrochemotherapy with either a diagnosis of mast cell tumor or soft tissue sarcoma. Grade was determined for all patients and recurrence free survival was stratified according to grade. Three hundred thirty-one dogs with mast cell tumor were retrospectively evaluated and two hundred and seventy-four dogs with soft tissue sarcoma were evaluated. This study obtained local control in both cutaneous and subcutaneous mast cell tumors as well as soft tissue sarcomas. The mean progression free interval in cutaneous mast cell tumors was 1825 days for grade I, 1803 days for low grade II, 902 days for high grade II and 817 days for grade III. Subcutaneous mast cell tumors were evaluated to be 1814 days for low grade and 1180 days for high grade. The mean progression free interval soft tissue sarcomas were 1432 days for grade I, 1000 days in grade II and 551 days in grade III respectively. Necrosis was observed at an average rate of 22% in mast cell tumors and in 18% of soft tissue sarcomas. Conclusion In this large study, electrochemotherapy decreased local recurrences after incomplete resection from surgery. The majority of publications are from European countries and this is the first evaluation of a large cohort of cases from the United States able to define overall progression free interval according to grade. Electrochemotherapy can offer a localized mechanism of control with minimal toxicity and continued use of this therapy is warranted in other tumor types.

title: Intraoperative technology in skull base and vascular neurosurgery: a two-stage cross-sectional national survey
abstract: Abstract Background: Skull base and vascular neurosurgery rely on diverse intraoperative technologies. Although many are well established, contemporary data describing real-world usage patterns across operative paradigms are limited. We aimed to characterise national practice and variation in intraoperative technology use within these surgical fields. Methods: We conducted a two-stage cross-sectional survey of UK and Ireland neurosurgeons via the Society of British Neurological Surgeons (SBNS). Six SBNS MedTech Committee members compiled a predefined technology list. Respondents then reported frequency of use of these technologies for three exemplar procedures: transsphenoidal approaches for pituitary adenomas, retrosigmoid approaches for vestibular schwannomas, and pterional approaches for intracranial aneurysms. Use was recorded on a four-point ordinal scale and analysed descriptively. Kendall’s tau-b rank correlation explored the relationship between surgeon experience and technology use. Results: Twenty-four responses from 21 British neurosurgical units (66% of adult/mixed units) were analysed. Technology use was strongly procedure specific. Neuronavigation was common for transsphenoidal surgery but less frequent for retrosigmoid and pterional approaches. Endoscopy displaced microscopy in transsphenoidal surgery, whereas microscopy remained dominant for retrosigmoid and pterional approaches. Indocyanine green video angiography and micro-Doppler ultrasonography were widely used for aneurysm vascular visualisation. Drills were common across procedures, alongside micro-debriders (transsphenoidal) and ultrasonic aspirators (retrosigmoid). Neurophysiological monitoring was universal in vestibular schwannoma surgery and variably used for aneurysms. Newer technologies, including augmented reality, exoscopes, intraoperative MRI, and robotics, were used infrequently. Surgeon experience showed no significant association with technology use. Conclusions: Intraoperative technology use in British skull base and vascular neurosurgery is strongly shaped by operative paradigms. Established technologies cluster around recurring procedural needs: orientation, visualisation, tissue manipulation, and neurophysiological monitoring. Newer technologies remain selectively adopted, with uptake likely influenced by cost, infrastructure, training requirements, and workflow compatibility.

title: Acquired Attentional Deterioration as a Diagnostic Pitfall in Child Psychiatry: A Pediatric Case of Possible Anti-GABABR Encephalitis With a Narrative Literature Review
abstract: Abstract Background: Attentional complaints are common in child psychiatry and are often initially considered within a primary attentional-disorder framework. However, acute or subacute deterioration in attention, functioning, or emotional state may warrant diagnostic reassessment, particularly when accompanied by medical or neurological red flags. Pediatric anti–gamma-aminobutyric acid-B receptor (anti-GABABR) encephalitis is extremely rare. This report describes a child initially evaluated for worsening attentional difficulties who was subsequently classified as having possible autoimmune encephalitis with serum anti-GABABR positivity, and provides a focused narrative review of reported pediatric cases. Case presentation: A 9-year-old girl had mild attentional complaints for approximately one year, with limited impact on academic functioning. During the month before admission, her inattention worsened substantially, accompanied by emotional changes and academic decline. She was admitted after an initial outpatient concern for a possible primary attentional disorder. After admission, electroencephalography (EEG) showed increased slow-wave activity, prompting reassessment of the clinical history and further neurological evaluation. A febrile episode approximately one month before admission was then identified. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)and routine cerebrospinal fluid(CSF) studies were unremarkable. In this case, EEG slowing was a non-specific but clinically relevant clue that prompted neurological reassessment. Pediatric anti-GABABR encephalitis showed sparse and heterogeneous evidence, with variable psychiatric and neurological manifestations.

title: Retroperitoneal Hybrid Nerve Sheath Tumor Mimicking Malignant Imaging Manifestations: A Rare Case Report
abstract: Abstract Background: Hybrid peripheral nerve sheath tumors (hPNSTs) is an exceedingly rare benign peripheral nerve sheath tumor, featuring elements from at least two nerve sheath tumor cells. We herein report a rare case of retroperitoneal HNST manifesting malignant imaging features. Case presentation: We reported a 40-year-old female presented with unexplained abdominal pain, with no significant personal or familial medical history. Imaging workup revealed a large solid-cystic retroperitoneal mass with internal hemorrhage, calcification and cystic degeneration. The lesion showed restricted diffusion and progressive delayed enhancement on MRI, with blurred borders adjacent to major retroperitoneal vessels and the right ureter, highly suggestive of an invasive malignant tumor. The patient underwent complete surgical resection. Postoperative histopathology and immunohistochemistry confirmed a benign hybrid schwannoma/neurofibroma, with no lymph node metastasis identified. The patient recovered uneventfully and remained recurrence-free during follow-up. Conclusions: Retroperitoneal hPNST can exhibit atypical imaging features that closely resemble malignant neurogenic tumors. Accurate diagnosis relies on the combined analysis of radiological findings and immunohistochemical results. This case expands the known anatomical and imaging spectrum of hPNSTs, improves clinicians’ overall recognition of this rare disease.

title: Reversible Adrenal Hyperplasia Associated with Chronic Etomidate Use: A Case Report with 3-Year Radiological Follow-Up
abstract: Abstract Background: Etomidate, a commonly used intravenous anesthetic, is known to reversibly inhibit adrenal 11β-hydroxylase (CYP11B1). Illicit electronic cigarettes containing etomidate have emerged in some regions, and chronic inhalation has been associated with acquired adrenal hyperplasia. However, the long-term reversibility of etomidate-induced adrenal hyperplasia after drug cessation has not been documented in the literature. Case presentation: We report a 33-year-old male patient who presented with recurrent fatigue, after approximately 10 years of 4-5 times per week etomidate-containing e-cigarette use. Laboratory evaluation revealed hypokalemia (serum K⁺ 3.37 mmol/L), normal morning cortisol (9.66 μg/dL), elevated adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) (322.00 pg/mL), and normal aldosterone-to-renin ratio. Computed tomography demonstrated bilateral adrenal thickening (9.3mm on the right, 9.5 mm on the left). Genetic testing excluded CYP11B1 and CYP21A2 mutations, supporting an acquired etiology. The patient was advised to discontinue etomidate use. At the 3-year follow-up, the patient remained abstinent. Repeat CT imaging showed largely resolution of adrenal hyperplasia, with adrenal thickness reduced to 3.9-4.3 mm bilaterally, and biochemical parameters returned to normal range. Conclusion: This case provides the first imaging evidence that etomidate-induced adrenal hyperplasia is reversible upon drug cessation, with largely radiological resolution documented at 3-year follow-up. The diagnosis of drug-induced adrenal hyperplasia can be established through a combination of exposure history, biochemical profile, and imaging findings, even in the absence of genetic testing. Early recognition is crucial to avoid unnecessary invasive investigations or genetic workup. A conservative "watch-and-wait" approach after drug withdrawal appears to be appropriate for similar cases.

title: Medial Epiphyseal–Epicondylar Alignment and Clinical Outcomes After Adding a Medial K-Wire to Lateral Two-Wire Fixation in Gartland II–III Pediatric Supracondylar Humerus Fractures: A Retrospective Cohort Study
abstract: Abstract Background Closed reduction and percutaneous pinning is standard treatment for displaced pediatric supracondylar humeral fractures, but the optimal pin configuration remains debated. We compared clinical and radiographic outcomes between lateral two-pin and medial-pin–augmented (crossed) fixation, focusing on the medial epicondylar epiphyseal angle (MEEA) as a comparative outcome rarely used for this purpose. Methods We retrospectively analyzed 202 children aged 2 to 12 years with Gartland type II to III supracondylar humeral fractures treated surgically between 2016 and 2021. Group 1 (117 children) received two divergent lateral wires plus one medial wire via mini-open incision; Group 2 (85 children) received two lateral wires only. The decision to add a medial wire reflected a mix of surgeon routine and intraoperative judgment of construct stability, not a fixed protocol. Outcomes were the Flynn rating, loss of carrying angle and elbow motion, and the Baumann, humeroulnar, medial epicondylar epiphyseal, and diaphysiometaphyseal angles, measured at final follow-up against the uninjured side. The Benjamini–Hochberg procedure controlled for multiple comparisons. Results Mean follow-up was 28.4 months; groups were comparable at baseline. Operative time was longer in Group 1 (40.7 versus 24.2 minutes; p < 0.001). Group 1 showed less loss of elbow motion (p = 0.008) and higher humeroulnar (p = 0.010) and medial epicondylar epiphyseal angles (p < 0.001) — the largest difference measured, remaining significant after correction; loss of carrying angle was also lower (p = 0.047) but not significant after correction. The Baumann angle and Flynn rating did not differ. No iatrogenic ulnar nerve injury occurred. Conclusions Medial-pin augmentation was associated with better-preserved alignment and motion at final follow-up. MEEA may detect medial-column alignment differences not captured by the Baumann angle, making it the more sensitive comparative measure here, without increased nerve injury. Because allocation was non-randomized, these findings describe an association rather than proof of superior fixation strength, and support selective rather than routine use of the added medial wire. Trial registration: Not applicable. This is a retrospective observational cohort study of a previously performed surgical treatment, not a prospectively registered clinical trial.

title: Machine/Deep Learning-Based Position Prediction of Pulmonary Nodules in Free- Breathing CT-Guided Lung Puncture: A Single-Center Prospective Cohort Study
abstract: Abstract Background Cranio-caudal respiratory drift of pulmonary nodules severely compromises accuracy of free-breathing CT-guided thoracic interventions, contributing to repeated CT acquisitions, prolonged procedure time, elevated patient radiation burden, and higher complication risks of pneumothorax and pulmonary hemorrhage. Conventional motion mitigation approaches such as breath-holding and respiratory gating require high-level patient compliance and constrain needle insertion to narrow predefined respiratory phases, which limits real-world clinical utility. This work addresses this unmet clinical need by developing and validating novel real-time artificial-intelligence prediction models. Leveraging only one baseline planning CT together with low-cost, portable nasal airflow and respiratory inductive plethysmography (RIP) signals, our framework achieves sub-millimeter prediction of nodule cranio-caudal position without additional dynamic imaging. Methods This single-center prospective cohort enrolled 139 patients with 143 nodules undergoing pre-VATS CT microcoil localization. Synchronized respiratory waveforms, paired CT scans, clinical, lesion and procedural metadata were collected. Nodule vertical displacement was quantified via Z-axis coordinate shifts of each nodule’s maximum cross-section geometric center. In total, 2275 paired CT datasets were split 4:1:1 for model training, validation and independent testing. Prediction performance was quantified using mean squared error (MSE). Results The nasal-airflow-driven SVM yielded validation/test MSE values of 0.099/0.166 mm², versus 0.120/0.186 mm² for ResNet-18. RIP-based SVM achieved validation/test MSE of 0.100/0.168 mm² compared with 0.122/0.198 mm² for ResNet-18. Across heterogeneous breathing patterns and lesion locations, absolute prediction errors of central Z-coordinates remained below 0.5 mm for all constructed models. Conclusions Portable respiratory monitoring coupled with machine-learning enables sub-millimeter nodule Z-position prediction without mandatory breath-hold or phase-locked gating. This solution can be directly integrated into existing manual CT-guided puncture workflows to improve procedural safety and efficiency with minimal additional hardware; it also provides an essential technical building block for next-generation robotic thoracic interventional platforms. Trial registration: ChiCTR2300068696 (2023-02-27)

title: Development and Internal Validation of a Prediction Model for Ureteral Access Sheath Insertion Depth During Flexible Ureteroscopy Based on Patient Anthropometric and Anatomical Parameters
abstract: Abstract Backgound:Optimal placement of UAS during fURS) relies largely on surgeon experience. Insertion that is too deep may cause ureteral injury, whereas insertion that is too shallow necessitates repeated fluoroscopic adjustment. This study aimed to develop and internally validate a machine learning model that predicts UAS insertion depth using the L1 vertebra–pubic symphysis distance and readily available anthropometric parameters. Methods This single-center cohort study enrolled 124 consecutive patients who underwent fURS with UAS placement between April 2025 and July 2026. The L1–pubic symphysis distance was measured on preoperative plain radiographs or CT scout images. Candidate predictors included height, age, sex, side, BMI and the L1–pubic symphysis distance. The outcome was the actual UAS insertion depth (cm), measured intraoperatively from the perineal skin to the ureteropelvic junction. The dataset was divided into training (70%, n = 86) and test (30%, n = 38) sets using stratified random sampling by sex. Six regression algorithms were compared, including Ridge regression, least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (Lasso), Bayesian ridge, random forest, support vector regression, and multilayer perceptron. Hyperparameters were tuned by five-fold cross-validation. Model performance was assessed using R², mean absolute error (MAE), root mean square error (RMSE), and the proportion of predictions within ± 2 cm of the actual depth. The final model was refitted on the entire cohort, and bootstrap 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were obtained for all coefficients. The study followed the Transparent Reporting of a multivariable prediction model for Individual Prognosis Or Diagnosis (TRIPOD) guideline. Results The mean UAS insertion depth was 33.7 ± 2.8 cm (range, 26.5–40.0 cm). Height (r = 0.749), male sex (r = 0.661), L1–pubic symphysis distance (r = 0.563), BMI (r = 0.251), and younger age (r = − 0.498) were correlated with insertion depth. Ridge regression with regularization parameter α = 10 achieved the best balance of accuracy and interpretability, with a test-set R² of 0.661, MAE of 1.24 cm, RMSE of 1.56 cm, and 78.9% of predictions falling within ± 2 cm. Five-fold cross-validation yielded an R² of 0.642 ± 0.067. Leave-one-out cross-validation across all 124 patients produced an R² of 0.649, MAE of 1.39 cm, and 77.4% accuracy within ± 2 cm, substantially outperforming an L1-distance-only model (R² = 0.291; MAE = 1.86 cm). Bootstrap internal validation (1,000 resamples) confirmed minimal overfitting (optimism = 0.026), with an optimism-corrected R² of 0.659, MAE of 1.39 cm, and a calibration slope of 1.033. Standardized coefficients identified male sex (β = 0.927; 95% CI, 0.651–1.205), height (β = 0.811; 95% CI, 0.444–1.148), and L1–pubic symphysis distance (β = 0.740; 95% CI, 0.396–1.086) as the strongest predictors, with BMI also contributing independently (β = 0.410; 95% CI, 0.164–0.674). A freely accessible online calculator was developed for clinical use. Conclusion A multivariable Ridge regression model incorporating the L1–pubic symphysis distance and anthropometric parameters can predict UAS insertion depth with clinically acceptable accuracy. The novel L1–pubic symphysis radiographic measurement, obtainable from routine preoperative imaging without additional examination, contributes independently to depth prediction. External validation in larger and more diverse cohorts is warranted before broad clinical implementation.

title: CAM-Threshold-Guided Weakly Supervised Lesion Segmentation and Relative Lesion-Burden Stratification of Wheat Stripe Rust Using CF2- WRD and Light-UNet
abstract: Abstract Accurate localization and quantification of wheat stripe rust lesions are important for phenotyping and disease management, yet dense pixel-level annotation is costly. We present a Grad-CAM-guided weakly supervised framework that reuses a dual-branch image classifier, CF2-WRD, to generate pseudo-labels for a compact Light-UNet segmenter. The dataset contained 34,694 images in 87 image-level categories, split into 27,834 training, 3,430 validation, and 3,430 test images. CF2-WRD achieved validation and test accuracies of 0.8776 and 0.8711. Among four CAM thresholds, 0.40 produced the highest agreement with CAM-derived validation pseudo-labels (mIoU 0.6584, Dice 0.7101, lesion IoU 0.5555), whereas 0.45 was used as a conservative operating point. Raising the segmentation probability threshold from 0.50 to 0.80 reduced mean predicted lesion-to-leaf ratio from 55.02% to 29.63% in a 300-image subset. The 3,430-image burden distribution was stratified by empirical quartiles. Because no independent manual lesion masks or expert-calibrated severity labels were available, overlap metrics quantify agreement with weak-supervision targets and burden groups represent dataset-relative rankings rather than agronomic severity grades.

title: Chronic Cerebral Small Vessel Disease Burden and Acute Infarction in Relation to Functional Brain Network Efficiency: A Cross-Sectional Resting-State fMRI Study
abstract: Abstract Background Chronic cerebral small vessel disease (CSVD) and acute infarction frequently coexist, but their respective relationships with functional network integration remain uncertain. We examined whether cumulative CSVD burden and clinical acute infarction were independently associated with resting-state functional global efficiency and explored which lesion phenotypes and anatomical regions showed the strongest associations. Methods This hospital-based cross-sectional study included 166 patients aged 45 years or older with suspected cerebrovascular disease. Automated multisequence MRI segmentation quantified white matter hyperintensities, recent small subcortical infarcts, lacunes, perivascular spaces, and cerebral microbleeds. Resting-state functional networks were constructed using a 90-region anatomical parcellation, with global efficiency prespecified as the primary outcome. HC3 heteroskedasticity-robust multivariable linear regression adjusted for age, sex, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, mean framewise displacement, and clinical acute infarction. Regional markers were jointly evaluated within each lesion family, with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction. Results Higher total CSVD burden was independently associated with lower global efficiency (B per 1-point increase = − 0.0055, 95% CI: −0.0086 − 0.0024; P < 0.001), whereas clinical acute infarction was not (B = 0.0008, 95% CI: −0.0071–0.0087; P = 0.850). The lacune regional block explained an additional 9.27% of variance (robust P = 0.00195). Parietal lacunes (B=-0.0130, FDR q = 0.026) and deep lacunes (B=-0.0132, FDR q = 0.021) were independently associated with lower global efficiency. Regional cerebral microbleed, perivascular-space, and white-matter-hyperintensity blocks were not statistically significant. Conclusions Greater cumulative CSVD burden, particularly parietal and deep lacunes, was associated with impaired functional network integration, whereas clinical acute infarction showed no independent association in this cohort. These cross-sectional findings identify anatomically informative correlates but do not establish causal or temporal relationships.

title: Ultrasound-Guided Paravertebral Nerve Block in Percutaneous Vertebroplasty: A Retrospective Analysis
abstract: Abstract Objective To retrospectively analyze the effectiveness of ultrasound-guided paravertebral nerve block in thoracolumbar fracture surgery. Methods Clinical data of 84 patients with thoracolumbar fractures who underwent percutaneous vertebroplasty at Xiaoshan District Traditional Chinese Medicine Hospital, Hangzhou, from July 2021 to July 2026 were retrospectively analyzed. Patients were divided into two groups based on the anesthesia method: the observation group (n = 42) received bilateral paravertebral nerve block combined with local anesthesia, while the control group (n = 42) received local anesthesia alone. The two groups were compared regarding intraoperative changes in heart rate (HR) and mean arterial pressure (MAP), Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) scores immediately post-surgery (T0), and at 6 hours (T1), 12 hours (T2), and 24 hours (T3) post-surgery, as well as postoperative complications and length of hospital stay. Results The retrospective study results indicated that, compared to the local anesthesia group, the paravertebral nerve block group had shorter operative time, more stable intraoperative MAP and HR, lower postoperative VAS scores, and shorter hospital stays.these differences were statistically significant (P < 0.05). No statistically significant difference was found in the incidence of postoperative complications between the two groups (P > 0.05). Conclusion Paravertebral nerve block anesthesia can stabilize intraoperative vital signs, shorten operative time, reduce postoperative pain scores, and demonstrates good safety.

title: Generative Artificial Intelligence for Opportunistic Osteoporosis Screening Using Lumbar Spine Imaging: Diagnostic Performance, Reproducibility, Effects of Few-Shot Prompting, and Comparison with Physicians
abstract: Abstract Purpose Osteoporosis remains underdiagnosed despite widespread availability of lumbar radiographs and computed tomography (CT). We compared physicians and multimodal generative artificial intelligence (AI) for opportunistic osteoporosis screening, focusing on diagnostic accuracy, reproducibility, and effects of few-shot prompting. Methods Forty-five lateral lumbar radiographs and 45 sagittal CT images were classified using DXA T-score thresholds of −1.0 and −2.5 as reference standards. Performance was compared among 42 board-certified orthopedic surgeons, 50 non-specialists, and ChatGPT, Gemini 3.1 Pro, and Claude 4 Opus. Each AI model evaluated all images five times under zero-shot and few-shot conditions, with 20 labeled reference cases provided for few-shot prompting. An exploratory analysis evaluated combined specialist-AI classifications using OR and AND rules. Results At the −1.0 cutoff, specialists outperformed non-specialists on radiographs (P<0.001). Claude achieved the highest radiographic accuracy (73.3%), followed by Gemini (64.4%), specialists (57.4%), ChatGPT (55.6%), and non-specialists (44.0%). Educational examples did not improve physician accuracy, and few-shot prompting did not consistently improve AI accuracy. However, reproducibility improved in several models, most notably Claude. An OR rule combining specialist and Claude classifications increased sensitivity to 80.0% on radiographs and 90.0% on CT, with reduced specificity. Conclusion Generative AI achieved physician-comparable performance under selected conditions but showed model-dependent variability. Few-shot prompting may improve consistency without improving accuracy. Exploratory combined assessment suggested complementary physician-AI errors may reduce missed cases at the cost of false-positive classifications. Generative AI may therefore serve as a decision-support tool for opportunistic osteoporosis screening but should complement rather than replace physician judgment.

title: Extent of Resection as the Primary Independent Predictor of Progression- Free Survival in Atypical Intracranial Meningioma: A Retrospective Single- Center Study of 187 Patients
abstract: Abstract Purpose Atypical meningiomas (WHO grade 2) show considerable biological heterogeneity and substantial recurrence rates despite surgical treatment, while reliable prognostic markers remain limited. We aimed to identify clinical and radiographic predictors of progression-free survival (PFS) in a large single-center cohort. Methods We retrospectively analysed 187 patients with histopathologically confirmed atypical intracranial meningioma (2016–2023), categorised by extent of resection (gross total resection [GTR] vs subtotal resection [STR]) and treatment strategy (surgery alone vs surgery plus radiotherapy). Kaplan–Meier and univariate/multivariate Cox regression were applied to identify predictors of PFS. Results GTR was achieved in 168 patients (89.8%) and STR in 19 (10.2%); tumor progression or recurrence occurred in 25 patients (13.4%). On multivariate analysis, extent of resection was the only independent predictor of shortened PFS (adjusted HR 3.09, 95% CI 1.14–8.37; p = 0.026). Peritumoral edema showed a consistent, non-significant trend toward shortened PFS (adjusted HR 2.43, 95% CI 0.92–6.37; p = 0.072). Age (HR 0.84, 95% CI 0.37–1.92; p = 0.7) and radiotherapy (HR 0.99, 95% CI 0.43–2.26; p > 0.9) were not significantly associated with PFS. Edema was not associated with the extent of resection or radiotherapy administration. Conclusion Extent of resection is the strongest independent predictor of PFS in atypical intracranial meningioma, reaffirming maximal safe resection as the central surgical objective. Peritumoral edema showed a consistent but non-significant trend that warrants confirmation in larger, adequately powered multicenter cohorts.

title: A Resource-Constrained Evaluation of Fine-Tuned Deep Learning and Local Zero-Shot Vision-Language Models for Brain MRI Slice Classification
abstract: Abstract Fine-tuned deep learning (DL) classifiers report near-saturated performance on public brain MRI slice datasets, but dataset leakage, lack of patient-level metadata, and limited robustness evaluation restrict their interpretation. Concurrently, multimodal large language models (MLLMs) enable zero-shot image understanding, yet their unadapted zero-shot performance under local hardware constraints remains unverified. We conducted a paired evaluation comparing fine-tuned DL architectures (ResNet18, EfficientNet-B0, ConvNeXt-Tiny, ViT-B/16) across three seeds against local zero-shot MLLMs (Qwen3-VL-2B/8B, MedGemma-4B) on a locked, leakage-screened 260-image four-class evaluation set using a single NVIDIA RTX 3080 GPU (10 GB). We evaluated ImageNet pretraining on ResNet18, executed a 35,100-inference controlled corruption matrix across five synthetic transformations, and compiled a frozen 24-case Grad-CAM failure gallery. Fine-tuned ConvNeXt-Tiny achieved the highest mean Macro-F1 (0.9610 ± 0.0041), followed by EfficientNet-B0 (0.9531 ± 0.0069), pretrained ResNet18 (0.9476 ± 0.0024), and ViT-B/16 (0.9284 ± 0.0157). ImageNet pretraining exceeded scratch training by +0.0617 Macro-F1 (95% CI [0.0077, 0.1192]; scratch seed SD 0.0515), though scratch models exhibited marked seed-level initialization sensitivity. The strongest local zero-shot MLLM (Qwen3-VL-8B) reached Macro-F1 0.3991, yielding a large observed performance gap under the tested zero-shot, label-only setting (McNemar p < 0.001). Under corruptions, ConvNeXt-Tiny had the numerically lowest mean Macro-F1 drop (0.0253). Grad-CAM maps revealed spatial shifts during perturbation failures, though focal maps were also observed in misclassified cases. Under constrained local compute, which restricts deployable model parameter scale, the tested fine-tuned DL models substantially outperformed the unadapted zero-shot MLLMs evaluated without task-specific fine-tuning on this slice-level benchmark. High in-domain scores must be interpreted conservatively alongside dataset provenance, corruption sensitivity, and post-hoc explanation limits.

title: Clinical Efficacy of Multiparametric Magnetic Resonance Imaging and Proton Spectroscopy in the Evaluation of Complex Ring-Enhancing Intracranial Lesions: A Four-Case Series from Pacific International Hospital, Papua New Guinea
abstract: Abstract Background: Ring-enhancing lesions (RELs) remain a persistent diagnostic challenge in neuroradiology, as neoplastic, infectious, and granulomatous processes frequently overlap in their conventional MRI appearance. Accurate differentiation is critical for guiding management, particularly in resource-limited settings such as Papua New Guinea (PNG), where access to advanced neuroimaging is concentrated in a few centers and specialist manpower is limited. Study setting and design: This retrospective case series was conducted at Pacific International Hospital (PIH), Port Moresby, PNG, over four months (June–September 2026). Four brain MRI cases were included: three presenting as ring-enhancing masses, and one miscellaneous nerve sheath tumour at the craniocervical junction and C1–C2 level. Materials and methods: Of the four cases, two were referred from Port Moresby General Hospital and two were managed in-house at PIH. Conventional MRI sequences, supplemented by single-voxel MR spectroscopy (MRS) in selected cases, were used to evaluate metabolite profiles and to help differentiate primary brain tumour, metastatic disease, and infective processes such as tuberculoma. Results: One case, an 18-year-old male, demonstrated a cortical high-grade glioma with elevated choline-to-N-acetylaspartate (Cho/NAA >1.5) and choline-to-creatine (Cho/Cr >2) ratios, favouring a glial neoplasm despite an atypical age. A second case, a 29-year-old male with constitutional symptoms, showed multifocal ring-enhancing lesions with a preserved NAA peak and Cho/NAA <1, consistent with CNS tuberculoma and correlating with the clinical history. A third case demonstrated periventricular, splenial, and parieto-occipital rim-enhancing and serpentine lesions, radiologically indistinguishable between tuberculoma and neurosarcoidosis; tuberculoma was favoured on supporting clinical evidence. A fourth, miscellaneous case demonstrated a craniocervical/C1–C2 nerve sheath tumour with a characteristic dumbbell configuration on T2-FLAIR and post-contrast T1-weighted imaging. Conclusion: This first PNG-based series demonstrates the added diagnostic value of MRS in characterising ring-enhancing lesions and illustrates how strengthened referral pathways from provincial and district-level facilities to centres equipped with advanced imaging can accelerate diagnosis and improve management outcomes.

title: Probabilistic three-dimensional mineralogical characterisation of drill core using μXRF and XCT: application to the Nautanen North IOCG deposit
abstract: Abstract Accurate mineralogical characterisation of drill cores is important for quantifying variability and supporting geometallurgical interpretations. Conventional assays provide bulk elemental concentrations but do not preserve mineral distributions, whereas individual non-destructive methods provide only partial mineralogical information. In this study, a probabilistic integrated framework was developed for three-dimensional mineralogical mapping, using four drill-core samples from Nautanen North, northern Sweden, as a case study. Micro-X-ray fluorescence (µXRF) maps classified with the Advanced Mineral Identification and Characterization System (AMICS) were co-registered with corresponding X-ray computed tomography (XCT) surfaces to derive mineralogical labels, which were used as two-dimensional supervision for a deep learning segmentation model, with XCT responses as the input. Detailed mineralogy was consolidated into four XCT-supported classes: Matrix silicates, Quartz, Garnet and Fe-bearing sulphides and oxides. Generalisation was evaluated using nested leave-one-sample-out validation, and predicted class probabilities were calibrated to better reflect prediction reliability. The selected support-aware calibrated ensemble achieved a mean accuracy of 0.899 and a mean macro Dice coefficient of 0.583. Matrix silicates transferred most consistently, whereas the Fe-bearing sulphides and oxides class remained difficult to discriminate because of its heterogeneous and overlapping XCT responses. The calibrated ensemble was subsequently applied to predict the mineralogical classes within a half-core XCT volume. Predictions remained spatially coherent across the evaluated XCT volume, with high confidence, low normalised predictive entropy and high spatial agreement. The framework demonstrates the potential to extend targeted surface mineralogical observations into three-dimensional predictions of mineralogical classes, accompanied by class probabilities and uncertainty fields, that can support geometallurgical domain definition and the selection of suitable samples for additional mineralogical analysis or metallurgical testing.

title: Longitudinal Multi-Modality MRI–Ultrasound Cyst-Level Analysis of Polycystic Kidney Disease in a Feline Model: A Proof-of-Concept Study
abstract: Abstract Polycystic kidney disease (PKD) in Persian cats is commonly monitored using total kidney volume (TKV); however, this kidney-level metric does not capture heterogeneity in individual cyst dynamics. Here, a standardized longitudinal imaging framework integrating volumetric magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with serial ultrasound (US) is presented, enabling cyst-level analysis in a feline PKD model followed over two years. MRI-based volumetry quantified individual cyst growth rates and identified structural coalescence events, defined as the persistent loss of visible boundaries between adjacent cysts without implying luminal communication. Serial US provided high-frequency temporal context and supported MRI-defined trends, rather than replacing MRI-based structural assessment. The analysis revealed marked asymmetric progression, with significant enlargement and coalescence of right-sided cysts, while left-sided cysts remained stable. This dual-modality approach demonstrates the feasibility of integrating volumetric MRI with serial ultrasound for longitudinal cyst-level analysis, enabling the identification of asymmetric progression and cyst-level structural remodeling that may be overlooked by kidney-level volumetrics alone. Although based on a single case, this study demonstrates the feasibility of a standardized MRI–ultrasound workflow and provides a methodological framework for future validation in larger cohorts.

title: Extension of the phenotypic spectrum of BMP1-related disorders through a novel homozygous variant identified in a foetus with intrauterine growth retardation
abstract: Abstract Background Osteogenesis imperfecta encompasses a heterogeneous group of heritable connective tissue disorders characterised by bone fragility and skeletal deformities. Autosomal recessive forms of OI may result from defects in the BMP1 gene, which encodes two main metalloproteinases, BMP1 and its longer isoform mTLD, both essential for type I procollagen processing. To date, BMP1 -related OI has only been reported postnatally. Results We report a complex homozygous BMP1 variant identified by prenatal whole-exome sequencing in a foetus presenting a polymalformative phenotype at gestational week 23 + 2.Ultrasound findings included severe intrauterine growth restriction, bilateral clubfeet, cranial bone anomalies, and signs of cerebral hypoplasia. At this developmental stage, histological examination did not show features of osteoporotic bone structure. A combination of molecular and biochemical strategies led us to characterise the variant and the consequences on BMP1 protein expression as its biological activity in the processing of several substrates. Functional in vitro assays demonstrated that the c.835A > G variant, located within the protease domain of BMP1, leads to (1) a deleterious missense substitution (p.Arg279Gly) affecting protease activity toward multiple BMP1 substrates, including procollagen I, thrombospondin-1, and chordin and (2) aberrant splicing, inducing exon 6 skipping, and a subsequent frameshift of the open reading frame. Conclusion This case broadens the phenotypic spectrum of BMP1 -related disorders and suggests a role for BMP1 in early human development beyond skeletal fragility. The findings support the inclusion of BMP1 in prenatal diagnosis gene panels for severe syndromic foetal presentations and underscore the importance of functional validation in variant interpretation.

title: Interpretable Machine Learning Using Normal Lung Radiomics and Dosiomics to Predict Radiation Pneumonitis After Lung Cancer Radiotherapy
abstract: Abstract Objective This study aimed to develop and interpret machine learning models based on radiomics and dosiomics features extracted from normal lung tissue after excluding the planning target volume for predicting grade ≥ 2 radiation pneumonitis within 6 months after radiotherapy. Methods A total of 232 patients with lung cancer who received radiotherapy between February 2023 and June 2025 were retrospectively enrolled and divided into a training set (n = 162) and a validation set (n = 70). The region of interest was defined as the whole lung excluding the planning target volume. Radiomics features were extracted from pretreatment contrast-enhanced simulation CT images, and dosiomics features were extracted from three-dimensional RT Dose files using the same normal lung region. After preprocessing, LASSO regression and random forest were used for feature selection, and their intersecting features were retained. Eleven machine learning models were trained using five-fold cross-validation and evaluated in the validation set. Model performance was assessed using AUC, classification metrics, confusion matrix, and decision curve analysis. Kernel SHAP was applied for global model interpretation. Results Among all patients, 97 developed grade ≥ 2 radiation pneumonitis, with an overall incidence of 41.8%. From 214 extracted features, 18 radiomics and dosiomics features were selected for modeling. Validation-set AUCs ranged from 0.725 to 0.812. LASSO and linear discriminant analysis achieved the highest AUCs, both 0.812; the 95% CI for LASSO was 0.708–0.917. The final LASSO model showed an accuracy of 74.3%, sensitivity of 58.1%, and specificity of 87.2%. SHAP analysis indicated that first-order, shape, and texture features jointly contributed to model prediction. Conclusion Radiomics and dosiomics features from normal lung tissue may provide complementary information for predicting grade ≥ 2 radiation pneumonitis after lung cancer radiotherapy. The LASSO model showed favorable discrimination and interpretability in the validation set, but external validation is needed to further assess its stability and generalizability.

title: Fusing Radiomics and Ultrasonic Features: A Superior Nomogram for Diagnosing Cervical Tuberculous Lymphadenitis.
abstract: Objective This study aims to develop and validate a radiomics-based nomogram derived from ultrasound (US) images for differentiating cervical tuberculous lymphadenitis (CTL) from non-CTL in the pre-biopsy setting. Methods A retrospective analysis was conducted on 287 patients with biopsy-confirmed cervical lymphadenopathy (116 CTL and 171 non-CTL), all of whom underwent conventional US examinations. The US images were randomly split into training and validation cohorts at a 7:3 ratio. Radiomics features were extracted from manually delineated regions of interest (ROIs) using PyRadiomics. Features with intra- and inter-observer ICC > 0.75 were retained. Significant features were selected via t -test and LASSO regression. A radiomics score (radscore) was calculated, and a nomogram was constructed by integrating the radscore with US features (necrosis, heterogeneous, and posterior enhancement). Diagnostic performance was evaluated using ROC curves, calibration curves, decision curve analysis (DCA), and the Hosmer-Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test. Results The nomogram demonstrated discriminative performance, with AUCs of 0.798 (95% CI: 0.738-0.858) in the training cohort and 0.756 (95% CI: 0.654-0.858) in the validation cohort. Its AUC was higher than that of the clinical US model (AUC: 0.764 (95% CI: 0.700-0.829) and 0.744 (95% CI: 0.640-0.847), respectively) and the radiomics-only model (AUC: 0.693 (95% CI: 0.621-0.765) and 0.611 (95% CI: 0.492-0.730), respectively). The AUC difference between the nomogram and the clinical US model was not statistically significant, but calibration and DCA confirmed its favorable clinical applicability and goodness of fit. Conclusion The US-based radiomics nomogram may help differentiate CTL from non-CTL and serve as an adjunct to pre-biopsy assessment. This approach shows promise for improving the pre-biopsy diagnostic workup of tuberculous lymphadenitis, although formal subgroup validation in pathologically early-stage cases is warranted in future studies. Unlike "black-box" machine learning models, this nomogram provides a clear display of each predictor's contribution, which makes the model easier to interpret.

title: Miliary Brain Metastasis with Perivascular Enhancement in ALK-Positive Lung Cancer: A Rapid Recovery after Concurrent Lorlatinib and Whole-brain Radiotherapy.
abstract: Miliary brain enhancement presents a broad differential diagnosis, and its combination with perivascular enhancement (PVE) suggests inflammatory or infectious conditions. We herein report the case of a 30-year-old man with ALK-positive lung adenocarcinoma who developed progressive nausea and impaired consciousness during corticosteroid therapy. Brain magnetic resonance imaging revealed miliary brain enhancement with PVE, initially suggesting infection; however, the cerebrospinal fluid and laboratory findings were negative. Brain metastases were suspected. Concurrent lorlatinib and whole-brain radiotherapy resulted in rapid clinical and radiological improvements. Metastatic disease should be considered in cases presenting with miliary brain enhancement and PVE, even when inflammatory or infectious conditions are suspected.

title: Comparison of Pointwise Encoding Time Reduction with Radial Acquisition (PETRA) MR-Angiography with conventional MR-Angiography-Sequences for Follow-Up of intracranial Aneurysms in a real-world cohort.
abstract: MRI follow-up of treated cerebral aneurysms is essential to detect remnants or reperfusion but contrast-enhanced MR-angiography (ceMRA) and TOF-MRA can be impaired by implant-related artifacts. Pointwise Encoding Time Reduction with Radial Acquisition MRA (PETRA) is a novel, non-contrast MRA technique with promising results for aneurysms treated with clipping or coiling. However, its performance in patients treated with other devices, including flow diverters and intrasaccular devices, remains unclear. This study aimed to compare PETRA with other MRA sequences with a particular focus on vessel visibility. Ninety-seven patients with 124 aneurysms treated with various endovascular devices or surgical clips were included. All patients underwent MRI including PETRA, TOF-MRA and ceMRA between September 2024 and February 2026. Three neuroradiologists independently rated aneurysm reperfusion, as well as image quality and the visibility of the parent artery and branching vessels, using 3-point scales. Artifact-related signal loss and signal reduction due to artifacts were measured in millimeters. Interrater reliability was determined using Fleiss Kappa. Vessel visibility was rated superior with PETRA compared to TOF-MRA, and comparable to ceMRA. Artifact-induced signal loss and impairment were highest with TOF-MRA, differing significantly from ceMRA and PETRA. Overall image quality was lowest with PETRA. Reperfusion detection did not differ among the MRA sequences. PETRA shows potential as a non-contrast MRA technique for follow-up of cerebral aneurysms, providing better vessel visibility than TOF and diagnostic performance comparable to ceMRA. However, its prolonged acquisition time and associated lower image quality currently limits clinical feasibility and real-world applicability. Further studies focusing on scan time reduction and cross-device performance are required.

title: Sex-Specific Regional Brain Morphometric Correlates of Neighborhood Socioeconomic Disadvantage in Clinical Neuroimaging.
abstract: Background and purpose Neighborhood-level socioeconomic disadvantage is associated with adverse brain morphometry, yet whether these associations differ by biological sex remain opaque. Here, we investigated sex-specific associations between the area deprivation index and brain morphometry derived from routine clinical MRI in a real-world clinical population. Materials and methods Intracranial volume-normalized regional brain volumes were extracted from T1-weighted MRI examinations performed in 2,863 consecutive clinical patients (median age 54 years [IQR 38-68]; 61.2% female) at a single academic medical center and associated community partners using an automated atlas-based segmentation pipeline. Exploratory factor analysis was applied to 131 regional brain volumes to identify latent neuroanatomical morphometric networks. Sex-stratified and interaction linear regression models examined associations between area deprivation index national percentile rank and each factor score, adjusting for age, with correction for multiple comparisons. Results Factor analysis identified five neuroanatomical morphometric networks: cerebellar (ML1), frontal/executive (ML2), subcortical-ventricular (ML3), medial temporal/limbic (ML4), and posterior cortical/visual (ML5). In male patients ( n = 1,112), linear regressions revealed that greater neighborhood-level socioeconomic disadvantage was significantly associated with lower factor scores on the cerebellar (β = -0.006, 95% CI [-0.009, -0.003], P < .001), medial temporal/limbic (β = -0.004, 95% CI [-0.007, -0.001], P = .01), and frontal/executive (β = -0.004, 95% CI [-0.007, -0.0004], P = .04) networks. No significant associations were observed in female patients (all P s ≥ .61). The interaction analysis was significant only for the cerebellar network (β = -0.005, 95% CI [-0.009, -0.001], P = .01; all other P s ≥ .07). Conclusions In a real-world clinical population, neighborhood-level socioeconomic disadvantage was associated with lower regional brain volumes across cerebellar, frontal/executive, and medial temporal/limbic neuroanatomical morphometric networks in male but not female patients; the cerebellar network was the only network to remain significant in interaction models. These findings suggest that the neuroanatomical correlates of neighborhood disadvantage may be sex-specific, and that sex-stratified analyses may be necessary to fully characterize the relationship between the social exposome and brain morphometry in clinical neuroimaging research.

title: Microstructural changes in deep gray nuclei following electroconvulsive therapy.
abstract: Background and purpose Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) is efficacious for the treatment of major depressive disorder. However, its underlying mechanism of action remains debated and may involve neurogenesis, changes in axon/synaptic density or glial cells. Restriction spectrum imaging (RSI) is an MRI technique that can resolve subvoxel microstructure, separating intracellular water from extracellular water, which can be further partitioned into hindered and free water. This technique can be used to determine whether ECT affects cellular microstructure through changes in signal contributions. In the present study, we aim to determine how RSI metrics change following ECT and whether these metrics correlate with clinical improvement. Methods RSI analysis of the Perturbation of Depression Connectome (PDC 1.0) diffusion MRI data for healthy control and predominantly right unilateral ECT patients. MRI studies were undertaken at baseline, 1-week post-treatment and 3-months post ECT (follow-up). Results Following ECT, right-sided RSI metrics changed in cortical and subcortical brain regions including right amygdala and right hippocampus between baseline and post-treatment. The hindered water compartment increased, the free water compartment decreased, and the intracellular compartment was unchanged. Post-treatment, volume increased in the amygdala and hippocampus, which partially resolved at follow-up, while right amygdala extracellular indices persisted. Changes in clinical symptoms did not clearly relate to volumetric or diffusion changes. Conclusions RSI provides imaging biomarkers that suggest extracellular water shifts with corresponding volume changes to be the predominant effect of ECT. Transient and longer-term changes in glymphatic flow may be one of the contributing, underlying mechanisms of action for ECT.

title: Massive Ascariasis Causing Extensive Jejunoileal Necrosis and Septic Shock in a Toddler.
abstract: A 2.5-year-old boy who had recently migrated from a northern highland area of Vietnam to the south presented with fever, diarrhea, progressive respiratory distress, and severe abdominal distension. He was referred in septic shock, requiring mechanical ventilation and two vasopressors. Emergency laparotomy revealed complete jejunoileal obstruction from a dense bolus of more than 100 Ascaris lumbricoides worms and approximately 70 cm of transmural bowel necrosis. Segmental resection, complete worm extraction, and primary end-to-end anastomosis were performed. Histopathology confirmed transmural hemorrhagic infarction consistent with ischemic necrosis from mechanical obstruction. The child recovered after intensive care, antimicrobial treatment, transfusion support, and a single oral dose of albendazole after postoperative stabilization and return of oral intake; he was discharged on postoperative day 20 and remained well at 2 months when a second single dose of albendazole was administered. Massive ascariasis should remain a differential diagnosis in children with acute abdomen in endemic settings or after migration from endemic areas.

title: Upper-Limb Ischemia Due to Distal Embolization from a Dissecting Axillary Artery Pseudoaneurysm in an Elite Overhead Athlete: A Case Report.
abstract: In overhead-throwing athletes, repetitive shoulder motion may cause intimal injury and pseudoaneurysm formation, most commonly involving the posterior circumflex humeral artery. An elite cricket fast bowler in his 20s presented with 6 months of left shoulder and hand discomfort, followed by rest pain and numbness of the fourth and fifth fingers. Duplex ultrasonography showed thrombosis of an axillary artery pseudoaneurysm with distal radial and ulnar artery embolization, and magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a 1.5-cm pseudoaneurysm at the origin of the subscapular artery. Surgical exploration revealed a spiral intimal dissection with organized thrombus. The pseudoaneurysm was excised, the intima was secured with tacking sutures, the axillary artery was repaired with a great saphenous vein patch, and thromboembolectomy was performed. The patient returned to work at 6 months without residual deficits. Delayed diagnosis may compromise limb salvage and functional recovery. Early recognition of vascular pathology is essential in overhead athletes.

title: Ruptured Giant Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm with Bilateral Giant Common Iliac Artery Aneurysms: A Case Report.
abstract: Giant abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAAs), often defined by a maximum transverse diameter exceeding 13 cm, are rarely reported. We report a case of multiple giant aortoiliac aneurysms comprising a ruptured giant AAA and bilateral giant common iliac artery aneurysms (CIAAs). A 59-year-old male was transferred to our emergency department with a ruptured AAA. Computed tomography angiography (CTA) showed a ruptured giant infrarenal AAA measuring 16.9×9.7 cm and bilateral CIAAs measuring 9.6×9.7 cm and 9.0×8.7 cm. The patient underwent successful open surgical repair with an aortoiliac bifurcated graft. An intraoperative left ureteral injury was immediately repaired by end-to-end anastomosis over a double-J stent. Postoperative CTA demonstrated successful graft reconstruction without leakage. The patient recovered without further major complications and was discharged on postoperative day 23. This case highlights the technical challenges of treating multiple giant aortoiliac aneurysms and demonstrates that emergency open repair can achieve a favorable outcome.

title: Effect of an Electronic Health Record-Integrated Clinical Dashboard for Radiologists on STAT Priority Chest Radiograph Reporting and Downstream Care: A Stepped-Wedge Cluster Randomized Trial
abstract: BackgroundChest radiographs (CXRs) are the most common imaging exam performed, but CXR reports can be nonspecific due to incomplete history, relying on vague terms like "opacities" to convey diagnostic uncertainty. We prospectively evaluated whether introducing a clinical dashboard with relevant patient information affects CXR report specificity and efficiency, report concordance with discharge diagnoses, and follow-up chest CT utilization. MethodsIn this stepped-wedge cluster randomized trial (NCT06785246), a clinical dashboard for radiologists was rolled out with user education sessions across 15 service areas of an integrated health system from June 2024 to June 2025. Emergency department (ED) and inpatient CXRs were included. A large language model (GPT-4o) was validated using a Delphi panel of three experts to classify report specificity and CXR report diagnosis. A subsequent model release (GPT-5.4) graded each CXR report impression as negative, specific abnormal, or nonspecific abnormal. It also judged whether an abnormal impression matched an ED discharge diagnosis. The primary outcome was the proportion of specific reports (negative or specific abnormal). Secondary outcomes were report-discharge diagnosis concordance, follow-up chest CT, antibiotic and diuretic orders, and CXR reporting time. Mixed-effects models adjusted for time, patient age, and radiograph view, with random effects for radiologists, facilities, and service area. ResultsThe trial included 404,860 ED and inpatient encounter STAT priority CXRs read by 387 radiologists (256,303 control; 148,557 intervention). The adjusted proportion of specific reports was 82.2% in control periods and 82.1% in intervention periods (difference, -0.10 percentage points; 95% CI, -0.53 to 0.34; P=.66). Among abnormal reports, concordance with a discharge diagnosis rose from 40.9% to 42.2% (difference, 1.24 points; 95% CI, 0.20 to 2.28; P=.02). Follow-up chest CT fell from 11.4% to 10.9% (difference, -0.55 points; 95% CI, -0.92 to -0.17; P=.004). Antibiotic orders (24.0% vs 23.9%) and diuretic orders (14.7% vs 14.8%) within 7 days did not change, nor did reporting time (difference, -0.8 seconds; 95% CI, -2.7 to 1.0). ConclusionsGiving radiologists EHR context through a dashboard did not change the specificity of STAT priority CXR reports or prescribing patterns. It was associated with small improvements in diagnostic concordance and follow-up CT use, without slowing reporting. Validated large language models make it feasible to measure report quality across a health system. Trial registrationClinicalTrials.gov NCT06785246.

title: Construction of a whole-brain segmentation pipeline for 0.35T neonatal MRI
abstract: BackgroundWhole-brain segmentation of neonatal low-field MRI is needed for regional volumetric analysis, but established segmentation systems are designed around different field strengths, contrasts, and age ranges. MethodsWe first applied complete end-to-end pipelines, including FreeSurfer, FSL-based processing, Infant FreeSurfer, FastSurfer, BrainSuite, SPM12/CAT12, iBEAT v2, the dHCP structural pipeline, and M-CRIB-S, directly to 0.35T neonatal T2-weighted images. Because those systems did not produce a complete 47-region output, we next tested released end-to-end AI segmentation models, including SynthSeg, FastSurfer, FastSurferVINN, and QuickNAT. These were highly sensitive to input format, contrast, voxel geometry, and the high-field training domain. We then decomposed the task into skull stripping, registration, super-resolution, atlas propagation, and tissue refinement and tested the available components individually. ResultsNo complete end-to-end pipeline or released AI model delivered a usable 47-region segmentation in direct application. Stage-wise testing showed that preprocessing, reconstruction, registration, atlas propagation, and expectation-maximization each solved only part of the problem. Their final assembly produced complete 47-region outputs across the neonatal cohort. ConclusionsDirect application of established pipelines was insufficient for 0.35T neonatal T2-weighted MRI. A stage-wise combination of compatible components provided the workable solution.

title: Neuroimaging of intimate partner violence can underrepresent the most affected survivors
abstract: Neuroimaging is becoming an increasingly prominent tool to understand intimate partner violence (IPV) and partner-inflicted brain injury (BI). Yet, by nature of IPV and partner-inflicted BI, those most affected may be the least likely to be eligible, participate, and produce usable data in neuroimaging studies. A critical question therefore remains of who is represented in neuroimaging research on IPV and related BI. Here, we examined representativeness at three major stages of neuroimaging sample construction using screening records from 352 women and a subsequent cohort of 207 enrolled women with lifetime exposure to physical IPV. At the eligibility stage, three in five women eligible for behavioral research were deemed ineligible for magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) at initial screening. At the participation stage, the 61 women who underwent resting-state functional MRI (fMRI) had more education, were more likely to be employed, and reported lower psychiatric and neurobehavioral symptom burden than enrolled women who did not undergo neuroimaging. Finally, at the quality-control stage following fMRI, motion-based exclusion disproportionately removed women who had sustained the most partner-inflicted BIs. Our findings empirically reveal that eligibility, participation, and quality control each bias the demographic, clinical, abuse, and BI burden represented in an fMRI sample, and therefore have key implications for generalizability. Measuring and reporting representation bias can help identify whose experiences are underrepresented in the evidence, and accordingly reduce the risk that IPV neuroimaging research understates the very harms it seeks to characterize.
